carving table for his European Hotel.

The dust was actually flying on Gay street
yesterday, the first for over two months.
It is hard to conceive of more beautiful
weather than that of Sunday and yesterday.
Snow foot deep was reported at Glen
Mary, on the Cincinnati Southern Railway
last Friday.

A splendid new pavement has been laid in
front of the elegant new business house of R.
S. Payne & Co.

Col. W. Y. White, a prominent citizen
of Abingdon, Va., died suddenly at Abing-
don yesterday morning.

The McGhee building, corner of Gay and
Asylum streets, lately occupied by R. S.
Payne & Co., is being fitted up for occu-
pancy by the East Tennessee National
Bank.

The Chancery Court has been adjourned
till 10 o'clock Wednesday morning Judge
Staley is holding Criminal Court. There
remains but little business in chancery be-
fore the close of the term.

The eminent singer, Phillip Phillips and
his son will give service of song at the
First M. E. Church next Saturday night.
Don't fail to hear them. The admission is
90, reserved seats 75 cents.

Mcintyre, Heath & Belmont's Minstrels ar-
rived Sunday afternoon from Dalton, Ga.,
and took rooms at the Lamar House, about
20 in number. They paraded the principal
streets at noon yesterday with their splendid
brass band, and made a fine exhibition.

Lieut. Thos. S. Plunket, of the United
States Navy, Brother of Dr. J. D. Plunket,
of Nashville was drowned while skating, at
Erie, Pa., last week. He was master aboard
the steamer Michigan. The remains were
taken to Nashville and buried Friday last,
with appropriate ceremonies.

Three days of delightful weather.

A new opera-house is rumored at Chatta-
nooga.

A few days of such weather as the past
would start the railroad works to booming
again.

Nashville's new custom house will be COM-
pleted ready for the furniture, by the middle
of next month.

Chattanooga Times: There were fully
500 laborers at work last week on the Red
Clay & Ooltewah Railroad, and the work is
progressing rapidly, and will be finished by
June. Tracklaying will not commence
until few days before the work is COM-
pleted. The work was scarcely damaged
by the rains.

A special from Memphis to Monday
Nashville American, says Thirteen cases
of smallpox have been reported to the
Board of Health within the past forty
eight hours. Fifteen cases in all have
been sent to the pest house, three of whom
have died.

Chattanooga Times: G. K. Patterson,
formerly of the East Tennessee road, but
now conductor on the Texas Pacific divis-
ion of the Alabama Great Southern, passed
through the city yesterday en route for
Jonesboro, where he contemplates spend-
ing several days among friends and rela-
tives.

It is rumored, says the Chattanooga
Times, that the Cole Syndicate has bought
the Griffin & Carrollton Railroad and would
build it through to Rome, using that route
to Brunswick instead of going to Atlanta.
The report is that Cole will build the
Macon & Brunswick road on to Atlanta, as
the law authorizing its sale demanded, but
instead of building from Atlanta to Rome,
he would run from Monticello, point be-
tween Macon and Atlanta, to Griffin and
Carrollton on to Rome.

A very important measure, known in

29. NOES. 11. a party vote, except that
Messrs. Maxey and Davis of Illinois voted
"Aye" with the Republicans. Mr. Mahoney
also voted "Aye." Mr. Morrill voted "No"
with the Democrats.

The tariff-commission bill was then pro-
ceeded with, and the pending amendment
offered by Mr. Bayard was lost by party
vote—ayes 24, noes 27. Mr. Cameron of
Wisconsin and Mr. Davis of Illinois voting
"Aye" with the Democrats.

The bill was then reported to the Senate
from the Committee of the Whole, and Mr.
Jones of Florida argued against the power
of CONGRESS under the Constitution to
regulate or interfere with the liquor traffic
in the States.

Mr. Sherman replied that the bill did not
propose any interference with the license
or sale in the States, but merely instituted
an inquiry as to the best mode of dealing
with the evils growing out of the traffic.
He thought it sufficient answer to the objec-
tion to say that information was needed
to enable Congress to deal with the District
of Columbia and the Territories and to regu-
late the revenue.

Mr. Maxey corroborated and elaborated
the view expressed by Mr. Sherman. The
number of the commission was fixed at
seven in order that the diverse sentiments
on the temperance issue might be subtly
represented, and the time within
which the commission shall report was
fixed at eighteen months.

After some further discussion the bill
was passed—yeas, 24; nays, 11. The fol-
lowing is the vote:

YEAs.—Messrs. Aldrich, Allison, Blair, Coke,
Conger, Davis of Illinois, Dawes, Edmunds, Ferry,
Frye, Garland, George, Groom, Hale, Harrison,
Hawley, Hill of Colorado, Hough, Lapham, Aldrich,
McMillan, Nation, Barney, Miller of California,
Mitchell, Morrill, Platt, Plumb, Rollins, Sawyer,
Sewell, Sherman, Teller, and Walker—35.

NAYS.—Messrs. Banyard, Hampton, Har-,
Jonas Jones of Florida, Morgan, Pendleton,
Pugh, Ransom, Slater, Vance, Warwick, and
Vess—14.

Messrs. Kellogg, Jones of Nevada, Vim-
dom, and Cameron of Wisconsin, in favor
of the bill, were paired with Messrs. Far-
ley, Williams, Davis of West Virginia, and
Jackson, who were against it. Mr. Brown
was paired with Mr. Saunders.

The bill provides for the appointment by
the President and confirmation by the SEN-
ate of a commission of seven persons, not
more than four of whom shall be of the
same political party, nor be advocates of
prohibition, to hold office not exceeding
two years, who shall investigate the alco-
holic liquor traffic, its relations to revenue
and taxation, and its general economic,
criminal, moral, and scientific aspects in
connection with pauperism, crime, social
vice, public health, and the general well-
fare, and who shall inquire as to the practi-
cal results of license and prohibitory legis-
lation. The commissioners are to serve
without salary, and to report within
eighteen months after the passage of the
act. An appropriation of $4,000 is made
for their expenses. A protracted struggle
for precedence of consideration of pending
measures in which the respective merits of
the tariff-commission bill, the Japanese
indemnity fund, and the precedence-
count measures were detailed at length, occupied the remainder of the day. A charge
by Mr. Beck that the protectionists were
seeking to delay action on the bill, and
that the Journals owned by them had
made ayas to that effect, was met
by counter-charges. Mr. Hawley as-
serting that the free-traders' programme
was to prevent any change in order that
the crudities and oddities of the present
tariff might remain available as material
for political arguments. Finally the tariff
bill was taken up and informally laid aside
as unfinished business for Monday. The
Senate then went into executive session,
and soon after adjourned until Monday.

Mr. Hiscock of New York, chairman of
the Appropriation Committee, reported the
Joint resolution appropriating $4,000, to be
immediately available, to enable the
Lighthouse Board to meet extraordinary
expenses in consequence of the wind in
the Mississippi river. Passed.

The House at 12:30 went into Committee
of the Whole (Mr. Davis of Illinois in
the chair) on the private calendar.

Pending the discussion of relief bill
the committee rose informally, and the
House passed Senate joint resolution au-
thorizing the Secretary of War to use
Government vessels for the transportation
and distribution of the rations furnished
by the United States to the sufferers by
the Mississippi overflow. The committee then
resumed in session.

When the committee rose several
relief bills were passed, among them one
for the relief of J. W. Screws of
Montgomery, Ala. The Speaker laid
before the House the following mes-
sage from the President, transmitting "A
report from the Secretary of State touch-
ing the imprisonment in New Mexico of Thomas
Shield, and two other American citizens.

The report states that the resolutions of
the House calling for information relative
thereto was transmitted to Minister Nor-
dean, who, it was alleged by Shields, took
no step to procure their release, and the
following telegram was received in reply:

"The statement of Shields with regard
to me is false. Learning they were arrested,
I brought the matter to the notice of the Sec-
retary of State for Foreign Affairs.
They were released, and were again rear-
rested a few days since for drunkenness
and disorderly conduct. Particulars by
next mail."

is worthy of careful study.

Ridge culture consists in raising our cultivated ground into ridges, the setting of our plants upon those ridges, and the cultivation of the ground afterwards as means of enrichment of the soil.

Small grain and corn are rot cultivated alike. With small grain the ground is thoroughly plowed and pulverized, after which the grain is seeded in broad rows six inches wide on top and twelve inches from centre to centre. Behind the seed distributors follow the shovels which take the soil from between the seed rows and cover the thinly scattered seed. This makes a ridge on the seed bed and by the same process leaves a furrow between the rows. By this plan we realize several important advantages.

Nature provides that every growing plant shall show its roots into the earth, and its top upward. The dividing line between the roots and the top is near the surface of the soil. If the plant be given deep cultivation and deep soil under the seed it will make strong growth and a strong plant. By ridging the depth of your soil is double, and at the same time your deepened soil holds its moisture.

In seasons of excessive rainfalls the ridges serve as sheds and the furrows as gutters to convey away the surface water. In slight rains the moisture is all retained, the thorough pulverization and the relation of the ridges and furrows making the conformation of the ground favorable to their retention. In this way deep reservoir is established from which the plants may draw their sustenance by capillary attraction.

Sunlight and heat are indispensable to plant growth, and on ridged ground the sun has more surface on which to exert its power than it can have on level ground. Your corn, tobacco, cotton, cabbage and other crops will therefore come to maturity weeks earlier than under level culture. That is but plain logical deduction.

I will briefly recount the points in which ridge culture is superior to the old methods:

1. By ridging, the depth of the soil cultivated is doubled, it retains moisture to that degree better, and its capacity to withstand drouth is accordingly doubled.

2. By ridging, we not only raise the plant out of the wet and cold, but we provide it an effectual under-drainage in excessive rainfalls. In light rainfalls, the preparation of the ground has in effect made soil sponge, that in drouth will yield its stored reserve of moisture.

In accordance with the call of the Executive Committee, the State Prohibition Convention met in this City, on Thursday last.

In the absence of the Chairman of the Committee, Col. W. L. Nugent, Dr. C. B. Galloway called the Convention to order and nominated Hon. H. S. Van Eaton as temporary President.

The following delegates were enrolled:

The Convention was permanently organized, the election of Hon. J. W. C. Watson, Presbit and Rev. D. A. Williams and Prof. Jones, Vice-Presidents; and Jno. T. Buck, E. L. Gillian, Secretaries.

A committee was appointed on Resolutions as follows: C. B. Galloway, W. A. Hurt, J. N. Abby, J. B. Gambrell, J. G. Johnson, J. Lucas, and A. Douglass. Which submitted report calling forth some discussion but which was finally adopted. One of the resolutions insisting on the use of revenue derived from saloons in sustaining the public schools on the ground that such use of this revenue was a shift of responsibility to the liquor, and was used by its advocates in its defense.

A Central Prohibition Union for the State was organized. This Union was charged with the organization of auxiliary Unions in every county. The officers of the Central Union are President, Col. W. L. Nugent; Vice-Presidents, J. J. Cox, J. W. C. Watson, G. W. Sayles, W. J. Taylor, J. G. Hamilton, J. N. Adams, J. B. Gambrell, E. L. Gillian, J. H. Holloway, and N. C. Steele; Corresponding Secretary, John T. Buck; Corresponding Secretary, Dr. R. J. Miller, and Treasurer, H. H. Hines.

About one-third of the delegates were present, and some of these made very earnest appeals in behalf of the Prohibition movement. The officers of the Central Prohibition Union were constituted an Executive Committee for all purposes.

A following preamble and resolution, read by Judge Watson, was unanimously adopted:

WHEREAS, The influence of woman is an important factor in support of every cause in law she enlists; therefore be it resolved That we appeal to our wives, our mothers, our daughters and our sisters to be most active workers with us in behalf of the regulation of the prohibition of the liquor traffic. To this end we urge them by present example, to do all in their power to ban the use of intoxicating liquor from their social circle, and from all festive occasions and we hereby cordially commend them. In every community the organization sign of woman Christian Temperance Unions has been formed. All county organizations of the Prohibition Union were urged to use all legal means for the enforcement of existing laws regulating the sale of liquors.

The real power in Egypt has been held by England and France, who have hordes of financial agents there to collect taxes for the payments of debts due these powers. These agents receive enormous salaries—$3,900 to $4,000, each—for their services, and live luxuriously, thus keeping the poor Arab in abject poverty.

Other nations, they say, have debts due other governments, and yet are not in the hands of those to whom they are indebted; hence they say, "Let Egyptians rule and govern Egypt." "Before these foreigners came here to protect us, we had better peace and greater safety than now." To-day there is a British Consul in every city in Turkey. Why? To protect Christians. But their presence only stirs up the Turk. He looks at the elegant dwellings of England's consuls, compares their condition with his own, grasps his sword, rushes into the street and defiantly plunges it into the first Christian he meets.

"Lost are the gallant three hundred, the Heavy Brigade!"

But they rode like victors and lords
Through the forest of lances and swords,
In the heart of the Russian hordes,
They rode, or they stood at bay,
Struck with the sword hand and slew,
Down with the bridle-hand drew
The foe from the saddle, and threw
Underfoot there in the fray.
Ragged like storm, or stood like rock
In the wave of stormy day,
Till suddenly shock upon shock,
Staggered the mass from without:
For our men galloped up, with cheer and shout,
And the Russians surged and wavered and reeled,
Up the hill, up the hill, up the hill, out of the field,
Over the brow and away.
Glory to each and to all, and the charge that they made!
Glory to all the three hundred, the Heavy Brigade!

example. the weight of broken rocks is

inches; you have therefore only weighed
nine inches of solid foot, and should
add one fourth of weight to correct total
that is l25 pounds.

The election in Ohio on Tuesday was for
three state otficers-Secretary of State, q
Judge of the Supreme Court and mem.
Der of the Board of Public Works-and for
members of congress. The issues involved
were such as generally divide the republi-
can and democratic party, although in the
course of the canvass Gov. Foster lugged
IN the temperance question, with full know.
ledge that thereby he would ALLEVIATE the
German vote but as fully expecting to more
than make up that loss from the strong
temperance sentiment in the rural districts.
His calculation, under ordinary cIcum.
stances, would have been correct. On the
temperance issue alone the rural sentiment
would have been sufficient to neutralIze the
German vote. But where Gov Foster made
his mistake was in making no allowance
for the loss of votes arising from the gen.
eral dissatisfaction with the republican
party that is abroad in the land from the
record of the last congress, the bad faith OF
its leaders in regard to promised reforms,
its extravaganza and general corfu ption.
Then no doubt theparty was also weakened
by the abuse OF the appointing power by
the "Guiteau President" who had 50 elo-
quently eulogised civil service reform in
his letter of acceptance; and further by the
infamous blackmailing system of the Con
gressional Committee through Jay Hub.
bell, with authority to state that there
would be no objection to the robbery III
official quarters, "a system which VI ques..
tloplbl1syffoo lost more votes than the huge cor.
rupuon fund wrung from the salaries Of
public servants succeeded in purchasing.


That the revolution IN Ohio is to he ac-
counted for largely in this way aside from
the loss Of the German vote is evidenced
by the fact that the falling off of the repub.
lican vote and the gains of the democrats
were uniformly maintained not only IN the
cities or IN German localities, but all over
the state. Even in the strongest temper
ance centers the republican vote is dimln-
ished and that of the democrats increased.
We are justified, therefore, IN setting down
the revolution IN Ohio as not mere TEN.
porary success arising from exceptional
) auses, but as square verdict against the
republican party which will be as perma.
nent as the party itself under Its present
leadership, principles and practices.


AS to the details of the victory, there is
no need to go into them infinitely. The

The brigantine Achilles, from Montevideo for New York, with hides, went ashore at Little Egg Harbor, New Jersey, yesterday morning in a thick fog and heavy sea. Her crew were saved.

The suspension of J. B. Ficklen & Sons, of the Bridgewater Mills, at Fredericksburg, Va., was announced yesterday. Their liabilities are announced at 1000.

The east wing of the Kings County Insane Asylum, at Flatbush, New York, was burned yesterday morning, and two of the inmates perished. The loss on the building is about $50,900.

The winning horses at the Augusta races yesterday were Farragut, Barney Lyon, Franklin Tom and Bonnie Castle. The third race was won by Lady Montague, but her rider having slipped her weights, it was awarded to Franklin Tom.

The Senate yesterday confirmed John W. New, of Indiana, to be Assistant Secretary of the Treasury, P. B. S. Pinchback, Surveyor of Customs, at New Orleans, Edwin H. Nevin, Surveyor of Customs at Philadelphia, John A. Caldwell, Assistant Appraiser at Philadelphia, and Wakefield G. Freye, Consul General at Halifax.

The deadlock in the Senate of Virginia in regard to the election of State Auditor, was broken yesterday by the adoption of the House concurrent resolution to elect Auditor, Railroad Commissioner, Corporation Judges, and judges of Appeals on Thursday. The vote was 19 to 17, and the result was reached by the return to their party allegiance of three Readjusters who had voted with the Democrats to postpone the election. Their action is regarded as insuring the defeat of Massey, and the choice of Allen, the Readjuster candidate.

The First National Bank of Baton Rouge, Louisiana, was yesterday authorized to begin business with capital of 500,900.

The National Bank of Mexico will be opened for business in the city of Mexico to-day. The Mexican Government has made deposit in the bank towards paying an installment of the American debt.

The thumb in China is regarded as a better means of identification than the face itself. Celestial vagabonds are not photographed for a rogue's gallery, as in this country, but their thumbs are smeared with lampblack and pressed down upon a piece of paper, thus furnishing rude impression, which is carefully kept in the police records. A face may be altered, say the Chinese, but a thumb never changes.

MR. JOHN COOKE, President of the Danforth Locomotive and Machine Works, and Vice-President of the First National Bank of Paterson, died yesterday. Mr. Cooke when only eight years old worked in a cotton mill, and as soon as he was old enough learned the trade of a machinist. Forty years ago he obtained work in the Rogers Locomotive and Machine Works, where his father-in-law, William Swinburne, was Superintendent. When the company was reorganized, in 1848, Mr. Cooke became Superintendent and four years later was admitted into the firm. Mr. Cooke's health has been falling for some years.

From Mr. W. A. Freeman's second article in The
Fortnightly Review for September

It strikes me that as the doctrine of state
rights was pushed to mischievous extreme twenty
years and more ago, there is danger now of the
opposite doctrine being pushed to mischievous
extremes. The more I look at the American Union the
more convinced am I that no vast region taking in
lands whose condition differs widely in everything
can be kept together only by Federal system having
large independent powers in the hands of the sov-
ereign States. No single parliament could legislate,
no single government could administer, for Maine,
Florida, and California. Let these States be left to
great extent independent, and they may remain
united on those points which it is well that they
should remain united. To insist too close union
is the very way to lead to separation. I know of no
immediate to fear any attempt at centraliza-
tion such as might thus lead to separation. But it
does seem a possible danger; it seems to me that
there are tendencies at work which are more likely
to lead to that form of error than its opposite.
Nothing can be a more matter of history than the
fact that whatever powers the Union holds holds
by the grant of the States. It is equally plain that
the grant is revocable, except if its terms
may be modified by constitutional amendment.
And the power of making constitutional amend-
ment is itself part of the grant to the States which
thus agreed that, in certain cases, a fixed majority of
the States should bind the whole. The errors of the
Secessionists lay in making an irrevocable grant in-
stead of a revocable one. The doctrine of the right
of secession, as a constitutional right, is absurd
on its face. Secession from the Union was as
at the time the original revolt of the Colonies
against the king. The only question in either case
is whether those special circumstances had arisen
which can justify breach of the ordinary law. But it
is pity, in avoiding this error, we run into the oppo-
site one, and to hold, not only that the grant made
by the States to the Union was irrevocable, but that
the grant was really made the other way and that
it is the received doctrine in quarters that the
States have rights into such as the Union allows to
them. One of the Boston newspapers was angry; he
ensued stated in one of my lectures the painful
historical fact that the States, in theory at least, are in-
dependent commonwealths, surrendered certain defined
powers to the Union and kept all other powers in
their own hands. The Boston paper was yet more
angry because large part of a Boston audience
warmly cheered, warmly, that it, for Boston, such
dangerous doctrines. I was simply ignorant; those
who cheered me were something worse.

Nowhere does the assimilating process go more
vigorously than in the United States. Men of various
nationalities are easily changed into good Ameri-
cans, and the good American must be, in every
sense that is not strictly geographical or political,
good Englishmen. And, regards large part, we
can give them other than a hearty welcome. The
German, and still more the Scandinavian, settlers are
simply men of our own race who have lagged behind
in the western march, but who have at last made it a
single pull, without tarrying for thousand years
in the Isle of Britain. But there are other settlers,
other inmates with whose presence the land one
would think, might lie happy, we dispense. I must
here speak my own mind at the great risk of offend-
ing people on more sides than men better versed
in American matters than myself point out to the
fact that the negro vote balances the Irish vote; but
one may be allowed to think that Aryan land
might do better still without any Irish vote, that
Aryan land might do better still without any negro
vote. And what venture to say on the house-top,
has been whispered in my ear in closets by not a few
in America who fully understand the state and the
needs of their country. Very many approved when
suggested that the best remedy for whatever was
amiss would be if every Irishman should kill men,
and be hanged for it. Those who dissented,
dissented most commonly on the ground that
if there were no Irish and no negroes, they
would not be able to get any domestic service.
The most serious objection came from
Rhode Island, where they have no capital punishment
and where they have no wish to keep it at the
public expense. Let no one think that I have any
feeling toward the Irish people in their state; I
have every sympathy with them. I argued long ago
in the pages of this review on behalf of Home Rule
and of any form of Irish Independence which did not in-
volve, some schemes then proposed did involve the
independence of Great Britain. I should indeed be in-
consistent to refuse to the Irishman what
they have sought to win for the Greek, the Bulgarian and
the Dalmatian.

The fact that the Irish element is in the English lands,
both sides of the ocean, is a mischievous element. The
greatest object of all for the severed branches of
English folk is to live in the fullest measure of freedom and unity that is consistent with their
state. Now, the Irish element in America is the
greatest of all hindrances in the way of this happy
state of things. It is the worst, and perhaps in
strongest, of several causes which help to give basis
to American politics. Political men in all
times and places lie under strong temptations
and do things which they otherwise would not do,
and do so in order to gain some party advantage. In
no on political men of any time or place has this kind
of influence been more strongly brought to bear than
it is on political men in the United States who will
grow and grow: no party, no leading man, can avoid it.
Parties and men are therefore
driven into courses to which otherwise they would not,
have to temptation to take, and those, for the most
part, courses which unfriendly to Great Britain.

Any ill-feeling which other courses may awaken between
the two severed branches of the English people
is prolonged and strengthened by the presence of
Irish settlers in America. In some minds they may
really plant hostile feelings toward Great Britain,
which would otherwise find place there. At an
rate they plant in many minds a habit of speaking
and acting as if such hostile feeling did find place,
a habit which cannot but lead to bad effects in many
ways. The more rumor, the mere thought, of re-
calling Mr. Lowell from his post in England,
even as in us that such things could
even have been dreamed of shows the baleful
nature of Irish influence in America and how spe-
cially likely it is to stir up strife and ill-feeling
between Great Britain and America, even at a time
when setting Irish matters aside, there is not in
the slightest ground of quarrel on either side.

The Irish difficulty is troublesome just now; it is
likely to be troublesome for some time to come; but
is not likely to last forever. But the negro difficulty
must last either till the way has been found out by
which the Ethiopian may change his skin or till
the white and the black departs out of the land.
The United States—and, in their measure, other part
of the American continent and sands—have to grapple
with problems such as no other people ever had
to grapple with before. Other communities, from the
beginning of political society, have been either
already practically founded on distinctions of
race. There has been, to say the least, some people, nation
or tribe which has given its character to the whole
body, and by which other elements have been assimi-
lated. In the United States this part has been played
so far as the white population is concerned by the ori-
ginal English kernel. Round that kernel the foreign
elements have grown and assimilated them; they do
assimilate it. But beyond that range lies another
eternal law of nature: the eternal distinction of color
forbids the assimilation of the negro. You may give
him the rights of citizenship by law: you cannot make
him the real equal, the real fellow, of citizens of
European descent. Never before in our world, the world
of Rome and of all that Rome has influenced, has suc-
ceeded an experiment been tried. And this, though in
ages of the Roman dominion the adoption and as-
similation of men of other races was carried to the ex-
tremest point, that the laws of nature would allow
the best way of citizenship on the negro is one which
shows what law can do and what it
cannot. The law may declare the negro to be
equal to the old question, am I not man and
brother? I venture to answer: No. He may be
man and brother in the same full sense in which
every Western Aryan is man and a brother. He
cannot be assimilated; the laws of nature forbid it.

And it is surely a dangerous experiment to have in
any commonwealth an inferior race, legally equal
to the superior, but which nature keeps down below it.
In this particular case because the Negro is a
whole peaceful and easily satisfied creature. He
has no very lofty ambition; he is for the most part
contented to imitate the ways of the white as
he can. A high-spirited people in the same case
would be a very dangerous element indeed. No one
pleads for slavery; but does the abolition of slavery
necessarily imply the admission of the emancipated
slave to full citizenship? There is, allowed difficulty
and danger in the position of a class enjoying civ-
il rights but not political rights, placed under the protec-
tion of the law but having no share in making the law or
in choosing its makers. But surely there is created
difficulty and danger in the existence of certain
class of citizens, who in the polling booth are equal
to other citizens, but who are not their equals any-
where else. We are told that education has done and
is doing much for the younger members of the
savage race. But education cannot wipe out the
eternal distinction that has been drawn by the hand
of nature. No teaching can turn a black man into
a white one. The question which, in days of con-
troversy, the North bowed with such wrath from
the mouth of the South: "Would you like your dau-
ghter to marry a negro?" is at the root of the
matter. Where the closest of human connections is
looked on as impossible, there is no
real brotherhood, no real fellowship. The attin-
tude of citizenship is in such cases mockery. An
I cannot help thinking that those in either hem-
isphere who were most jealous for the emancipation
of the negro must in their heart of hearts, feel a shudder
at the thought that, though morally impos-
sible, it is constitutionally possible that two years
hence black men may be chosen to sit in the seats of
Washington and Garfield.

An acute American friend pointed out to me the
distinctions between the three races which give rise
to the difficulties that beset the United States in
the matter. The Indian dies out. The negro is very
slow from dying out; but he cannot be assimilated
to the white man, he at least initiates him. But
a Chinaman does not die out; he is not assimilated;
he does not imitate; he is too fully convinced of
the superiority of his own ways to have the least thou-
ght of copying ours. The Chinese, in short, in the United
States, belong to one of those classes of settlers who
form part of the people of the land, who contri-
bute nothing, but who swallow up great areas. Now,
it is not so.

Yesterday was the day set for the convention of the Republicans of Knox, Anderson and Loudon Counties, in this city. The senatorial convention was organized at the court house, by the election of G. B. Gossett, as chairman, and J. H. York, secretary.

A committee on credentials was appointed. When it was ascertained that, owing to misunderstanding as to the date of holding the convention, no delegates were present from Anderson County, the convention adjourned until Saturday, September 30th.

The second convention was then called to order and organized, with G. B. Gossett as chairman, and J. A. Swan secretary. The following committee on credentials was appointed: W. F. Yardley, J. H. York, J. Z. Reeder, Henry Haynes and James Dowell. The committee retired and soon returned and reported list of delegates, none from Loudon County being present. The report of the committee was adopted.

On motion, it was ordered that the vote for voter be taken by districts. Nominations being in order, DR. J. T. Shipley, of Loudon, and Capt. J. D. Bearden, of Knox, were placed in nomination for voter.

Chairman Gossett appointed ex-Deputy Sheriff George Brown as proxy to cast the vote of Loudon County.

An election was then had, which resulted in DR. Shipley receiving 11 votes and Capt. J. D. Bearden 9 votes.

A motion was made and carried making Capt. Bearden's nomination unanimous. On motion of W. F. Yardley, Esq, the chairman appointed committee consisting of W. F. Yardley, Esq, and J. W. Payne to wait on Capt. Bearden, inform him of his nomination and escort him to the speaker's stand, which duty was performed by the committee.

Captain Bearden addressed the convention, thanking them for the honor conferred in nominating him as their candidate for voter. He stated that the county of Knox had twice before honored him with nomination, and he had twice carried the Republican banner to victory, and hoped to do it again. He defined his position on the State debt question was in favor of more money for free schools and favored a change in the road law, having less road overseers and more money for the roads.

He was loudly applauded. The chairman was instructed to appoint a voterial committee, and announce the same through the city papers. The convention then adjourned sine die.

The convention to select two candidates for representative was called to order by J. A. Swan, chairman of the county Republican executive committee, and organized by electing J. H. York chairman, and James Z. Reeder secretary.

A committee of five on credentials was appointed, who returned long list of delegates. The report of the committee was adopted.

The following nominations for representative were made: W. D. Rule, A. L. Cottrell, DR. S. W. Kennedy, W. F. Yardley and John H. Nelson.

Esq. Yardley took the floor and requested that his name might be withdrawn, as this was not the time for him to come before the people for Legislative honors, but hoped that in the near future the millennium might dawn for the colored race, and white Republicans and Democrats would feel honored in supporting with their votes colored man in office.

In voting for candidates by districts, it was, on motion, ordered that the two candidates receiving the highest number of votes should be declared duly nominated. The election was then gone into, with the following result: W. D. Rule, 30; DR. S. W. Kennedy, 20; A. L. Cottrell, 9.

A motion was carried to make the nomination of Rule and Kennedy unanimous. The chairman was instructed to appoint a county executive committee and announce the same through the city papers.

The convention then adjourned sine die, amid loud calls for Rule and Kennedy, who failed to respond.

The great forensic effort of the 27th Congress of the United States in 1829 was the fulsome burst of oratory of Mr. Webster on the Foot resolutions, more excellent in its delivery than in its results. The great speech of the 47th Congress in 1882 was the able argument of Mr. Carlisle of Kentucky upon the tariff, demonstrating with mathematical precision the astounding fact that under the disguise of revenue tariff, 10,000,000 of people of the United States are annually paying tribute of 45 per cent of the clothes they wear and implements of agriculture they use to the enrichment of an aristocracy. Oratory has ceased to be defamation and gesture, and has become argument and reason based upon research and investigation.

This is noticeably so in new countries where once the impulse of bold adventure and thrilling exploits impaired their spirit to the hustings and the bar, but where now commerce and exchange have brought the country to the basis of purely business dealings. We must here in the south realize and teach young men that rhetoric must be subservient to mathematics, fiction to historical truths, oratory must yield to argument, faith to securities, and that the great object of education is to make of boys business men.

It is not education alone that makes men, but it is the use to which they put it. Your teacher may impart to you information, he may take you through the course of a finished education embracing the languages, sciences, classics and mathematics complete, but their application and utility is alone in your hands. The knowledge received by you is education, the use you put it to is business. Without the latter the former is useless, and perhaps you would be better off without it, for then, at least, you would be content to labor with your hands if necessary. The two combined make the great men of the country and of course the more excellent the elements of the combination the greater the man. That youth on foot upon the highway, carrying on his back a peddler's pack, is but an immigrant Hebrew. He scarcely speaks the English language intelligibly. The young gent with polished boots and Havana cigar, who stands upon the streets and jeers as the foreigner passes, has conquered the entire curriculum of college. He is an A.M. Six months have passed and our Hebrew boy rides in vehicle and vends peddler's wares. Six months more and he is ensconced in a small business house and buys all the hides, feathers, old iron and ginseng he can lay his hands upon. A year or so more and we find him a useful naturalized citizen, doing a prosperous business on the public square, and our young A.N.J., perhaps of ante-war aristocracy, begs at his door for employment at $40 per month. Here is business and education, each without the other. Which of the two would you prefer? Let your answer be, neither but both.

A gentleman not long since living not far from here, largely engaged in manufacturing, said to me that after repeated and earnest efforts he was absolutely unable to obtain native born southern young man who was willing and able to take and fill an important post in his enterprise, where thousands of dollars were invested and large salaries paid to the principal employees. Not that they lacked education, but they lacked the business qualifications or the willingness to acquire them. He found young men who promised and some who entered upon the discharge of the duties, and did well for a week or a month or so, but when the ordeal came, requiring long, arduous and unremitting watch, or close and accurate transactions, the crucible period too severe, they fell by the wayside, and he was forced to send to the east or to England for a man and the first chosen filled the place without flinching. On a visit to East Tennessee last summer it was my lot to visit several large manufactories where eastern and even English capitalists had invested millions of dollars, and as I now remember, not a single native southern-born young man held a high position in either of them. You ask them why and they will reply "We cannot find a young man here who will stick to business." Now, as reason for this, some will say it is sectional prejudice, and curse the war, but let me say to you, the fault is at our own door. Show me a young man of the south who has developed fine business qualifications who has ever failed to obtain employment anywhere, and especially of northern or eastern persons. How many are there in New York to-day?

A short time since a number of us were engaged in an immigration movement, to induce industrious immigrants to come among us, to buy and till the countless acres of rich soil in Giles county, and an intelligent excellent farmer accosted me on the street and challenged the movement, upon the grounds that if those fellows came among us they would crowd our own people out. What commentary on our own native-born patriotic southern people! The idea is fallacy. We need the thrifty, industrious immigrant among us, and our arms should be wide open to receive them. Wherever they have settled among us they have exhibited examples of industry and thrift, and in aid of support of educational institutions well-worthy of our emulation, and I challenge any man to look around him and find an instance contradictory of this statement.

Rodney, of Austin, Texas, sent twenty of these pennies to the United States Assay Office in this city, with the information that the pennies were being bought up at six per hundred by speculators on the supposition that they contained gold. On the contrary, while gifted with unusual abilities for public life that were early recognized in his career, he was nearly, if not quite fifty years of age, before he was appointed from the supreme bench, where he had served eighteen years, to the United States senate. Up to this time certainly Judge Poland has not been in active politics. He served eight years in congress—and was only beaten in his fifth term by a fusion of democrats with faction of sorehead republicans. Judge Poland has never posited as philanthropist, nor a swivel service reformer, but we fail to see what proof there is that he has been supremacy selfish man in politics beyond that ordinary difference to self-interest that all men manifest in all the pursuits of life. In the sense that all men, who are part of the breathing, working world of politics and business, are selfish, we suppose Judge Poland has struggled to deserve and achieve success, but this is true of all men of any ambition who ever accomplished anything for themselves or others. Abraham Sheetner, only a short time since prosperous shoemaker in Warsaw, about a year ago had his home entered by a mob of peasants, who seized his wife and three children and bore them to the outskirts of the hamlet, while the father, frantic with grief, vainly followed, pleading for his loved ones. The jeers and shouts of the incarnate fiends were the only reply to his supplications. On reaching the suburbs of the hamlet street poles were planted in the earth so as to form a group of the mother and children. The innocent victims were bound to the stake, their clothing saturated with oil, fagots placed around their feet, and the torch applied. Almost within touch of his hand the father was bound to another stake to witness the hellish torture of his wife and children, who in vain stretched out their hands to him who could no longer afford them succor. The flames burned out with mock solemnity Sheetner was released and informed that he was at liberty to take charge of the charred trunks of what but few hours before constituted his loved and loving family.

Nurtulle Riskoff, lass of eight years, and the picture of health, tells the following story of the unnatural estrangement of a son and father through the son embracing the faith of the Gentiles: Her father was a watchmaker, and engaged with him was a son named Cabassa, who thought his father treated him unkindly. Cabassa embraced the faith of the Gentiles and spent his leisure time in their society. His father demonstrated with him, but to no purpose. The son had become enamored of a Gentile maiden. One afternoon the son left his home, and on the night of the same day returned with a party of Gentile companions. The father was taken from his bed, a small iron was heated to white heat, and, while the other tormentors held the father as in vise, the son thrust the iron into his father's eyes. The next day the son married the Gentile, and within a year the father died in poverty. The unfortunate child is with her uncle and aunt.

Israel Balaghor was in Odessa when the persecution commenced there in May last. He says that peasants attacked their houses and robbed them of their entire contents. The men were beaten and some killed. Women and children were assaulted. Even innocent babes were thrown out of upper-story windows, and their brains dashed out on the pavement below. A wealthy farmer named Beraski offered 10,000 roubles to the howling mob who had attacked his dwelling to spare his wife and daughters from outrage, but the fiends assaulted his family and beat him almost to death.

Isaac Vizier, of Warsaw, says violent demonstrations occurred in December last. Citizens at first attempted to defend themselves, finding it was useless to appeal to the authorities. They armed themselves with clubs, and for a time were successful in repelling the mob; but when this fact became known to the authorities the police swooped down upon them and demanded their arms, which were given up. Then the prosecuted people were left to the mercy of the heartless inquisitors. Children were thrown out of third story windows, men were murdered, children slaughtered, and the women suffered nameless horrors. Shops were turned out and houses pillaged and burned, while the police and military stood by without offering any interference. Four hundred more of these long suffering people are expected here next week.--Philadelphia (Fed.) Special (Feb. 22) to Chicago Tribune.

Vaughan, enclosing a retainer of one hun-

Library and Literary Association.
On Monday evening January 10, a meeting was held in the office of J. C. Ralph Snyder, Esq., for the purpose of effecting an organization, the object of which should be the establishment of a Public Library in the Town of Emerson and the cultivation of literary tastes.

The meeting was well attended, and Prof. A. W. Frederick was made President pro tem, with H. W. McCreary, Secretary. After certain preliminaries, a committee, consisting of Messrs. T. J. Cregan, J. O. Ralphsnyder and John N. Crane, was appointed to draft a suitable Constitution and By-Laws, when the meeting adjourned to meet at the Exchange Hotel Saturday evening, January 15, at which time and place a meeting was held and a Constitution and By-Laws adopted, and a permanent organization effected by the election of the following officers.

President—George Purcell.
Vice-President—J. G. Ralphsnyder.
Recording Secretary—T. J. Cregan.
Treasurer—Peter W. Smith.
Librarian—J. O. Ralphsnyder.
Corresponding Secretary—John N. Crane.

Select Reading—Boyd O. Stone, T. J. Cregan and John G. B. Jackson.
Question—N. J. Squires and T. G. Ralphsnyder.
Essay—Peter W. Smith and J. G. Ralphsnyder.
Original Oration—J. G. Ralphsnyder.

The organization saw the forming of the Emersonwood Library Association, and the commencement of that object which we desire to assist by the assistance and encouragement of the entire community.
